How One Should Artfully
Couch/Remove the Cataract.
Suffusio, Cataracta, or
Staan [Cataract]
I have already reported previously what
a cataract [Staan] is, insofar as it comes
into the eyes, and also how one should distinguish good and
bad defects from one another.
Now we will make the beginning
of how one should artfully undertake such
a work.
First you must know: when one wishes to undertake
such a thing, it must happen at the right time—
not in hot summer, nor in cold winter,
but in spring or autumn, on a
bright, fair, and wind-still day; not in
hot summer, lest an inflammation and
pain, fever, and restlessness might arise;
not in winter, because at that time healing is
slow and the injured part must suffer
longer.
It should take place in the waning moon [☾], because☾ = Luna / Moon.
the humors are not full/turbulent and
settle. Let the needle be in all, with the handle, 5
fingers long—the handle 3 fingers, the needle 2
fingers; it should not be too thin nor too sharply pointed,
so that one does not pierce the uvea or
cornea or crystalline therewith; it
should be very smooth and finely polished. Let the needle
be made of gold, silver, or steel.
NB: Know also that several oculists begin
such an operation 3 or 4 days
before the full moon.

Couches the Cataract Are the Following:

frau], or Aquarius [?]; afterwards are the following

Cataract Needles Should Be

Toward the point they should be finely even,
and at the tip smooth and round
and not overly sharp-pointed, still less
cutting, but should be like a good
tailor's needle; as for the handle, it may
be of silver, whalebone [fisch], wood, or bone/ivory, according to
your pleasure and liking.
How the Patient Should
Conduct Himself During the Cure.
When one has laid the patient in bed,

one should lay his head nicelyContinues from p. 71 col. B l. 24.
high, and for 2 hours give him nothing to
eat or drink; afterwards,
however, one may give him a good broth,
and then nothing more until evening;
afterwards one may again give him a
broth and a soft-boiled egg therewith, and therewith
he should make do until the next morning.
Yet in the evening he may well drink a
little mild and watered wine; however, it is
better to drink a boiled water of fennel, licorice
wood, and mastic, or a little cinnamon.
The next day he may eat and drink
in the evening when he will; only the
foods should be none that require much chewing
and mastication, but should be quite
mild soft foods, such as nourishing broths,
thin panada, small birds and the like, almond soups,
soft eggs, strained barley—he should make do with all these
until the 8th or 9th day. The patient
should sit propped up, and someone should
hand him his food; the patient should also
guard as much as possible against sneezing
or coughing, which is exceedingly harmful, and should
take great care not to talk much
or loudly; also that one make no hammering,
knocking, or any loud commotion in the
room.
And if he should wish to go to stool, he should
not stand up, but be assisted with a bedpan,
in such manner that one moves the
patient gently.
Above all, the physician should apply his due
diligence, and bandage the patient at the proper
time, 3 or 4 times a day, according as
the day is short or long, and in the same
manner as is described separately for each
cataract.
One should also keep the room wherein the patient
lies dark, and let neither candle-light nor fire
be brought to him; one may also set him up
every 3 days and let him sit for half an hour,
also remake the bed a little, and then
gently lay him down again into the same
bed.

Which Eyes Are Dangerous to CurePage number '72' in upper-right corner.
by Means of the Instrument
[Six Contraindications]
1. [Hard] to help are people who are
afflicted with epilepsy and the falling sickness.
2. Those who have fever and hot pains, or are
prone to vomiting.
3. Those who have narrow and deep-set eyes.
4. Those who squint [strabismus] and are cross-eyed
or have trembling eyes [nystagmus].
5. Women who are pregnant, or who have recently
weaned their children from the
breast.
6. All women who have their monthly
courses, or will soon get them,
or those who do not have them at all.
Of the Cure of the White
Cataract —
As soon as one has couched the cataractLarge ornate calligraphic initial 'S'.
in its proper place, take the instru-
ment out of the eye, and let the patient
sit quietly for a moment to give him peace,
and then gently open the eyes; meanwhile
if the patient, when he looks up, is still
blind as before, it is better to wait
and bandage the patient right away
and convey him to bed; thus for the first
time apply the following bandage:
The First Bandage for the
White Cataract.
Take [℞] egg-whites, no. 6; chicory water [▽] 2 oz [℥ij];
beat the egg-white well, then pour
the water [▽] therein, stir it well together,
and apply with a flax/tow pledget, as the following
figure shows. The pledgets should be well
moistened and squeezed out again, so
that it does not drip much, and lay on each closed
eye one, and bind it with a bandage
fairly firm and tight.

Figure of the Flax PledgetsPage number '73' in upper-left corner; labeled '#.o 10.' below.
These pledgets should be of good hackled flax,
and not of hemp, for hemp is very
harmful to the eyes; it causes great pain in
head and eyes. The little cloths and pledgets should
be diligently cleaned, and whenever one bandages,
one should take fresh ones; the cloths and pledgets
should always be wrung out in fresh water;
afterwards put the proper medicine thereon,
and with several dressings [apply] every
morning and evening for 2 or 3 days in
succession; then use the following
water [▽], as follows:
Water for the White Cataract
Take [℞] chicory water [▽], fennel water, lily of the valley,
of each ½ oz [℥ß]; mix, lay it with a fine little cloth
upon the eyes, and upon the cloth lay a fine
pledget; apply this twice every day, and when the
day is long, 3 times, until the end of the cure.

Cure and Healing of the Gray
Cataract, etc.:
The first bandage as described in the white cataract
is also good in the gray cataract:
Take [℞] egg-whites, no. 6; rose-water [▽] 2 oz [℥ij]; beat
the egg-white well, mix the water [▽] therein, and
apply with flax pledgets, as was shown in the white
cataract; use it 2 or 3 days in succession,
then use the following water [▽]:
Water for the Gray Cataract
Take [℞] rose-water [▽] 6 oz [℥vj], fennel water [▽] 4 oz [℥iiij]; mix, and apply
with flax pledgets and 4-fold little cloths, as
the following figure shows; this should be done every day
2 or 3 times, according as the day is short or
long.Portrait labeled '#.11.' below.
The physician should also allow no women near,
to bandage the patient, but should
do it himself when he has time, or entrust it to a
male person, and apply diligence and
cleanliness in all of this.

Here Follows Further Concerning Band=
aging the Cataract.
So that one may have a complete report, and
handle the matter rightly, you should know that all
operated cataracts should not be kept bound with the first
bandage longer than 2 or 3 days; twice a day,
evening and morning, or when the day
is long, bandage 3 times. On the 3rd or
4th day one should gently let the patient
sit up; also if necessary
have the bed remade, and gently let him
sit upon the bed, provided he keeps his head
leaning back; where it is not necessary,
he may well remain lying. Let the patient then
open his eyes a little, yet so that
he does not look into the light; and wash them with
the proper water [▽] cleanly out,
and bind them with the proper flax pledgets
and cloths and water [▽] again; with this one should
continue for 4, 5, or 6 days, accord-
ing as the cataract is young or old, light or
heavy. If a cataract is young or light,
I have let it lie bound 10, 11, or 12 days;
if, however, a cataract is old and heavy, I have
not let them lie bound past 6, 7, or 8 days. And
even when one has nearly completed the cure,
one should still every evening for 5 or 6 days
lay moist cloths upon the eyes
until he grows accustomed to the light.
When now the time—such as 6, 8, 10, or 12
days—has passed, I have first let them
sit down in bed for a day, keeping the head
upright, and keeping the room still
darkened. The next day I have
let them sit gently upon a stool,
and occasionally walk to and fro in the room;
on the third day a little better, and
so forth; and let light into the room a little
more each day. Yet before 3 or 4
weeks they should not look into any fire-flame or stove-glow,
for it is exceedingly harmful,
and they should always wear in the dark cure

a little cloth hanging before the eyes, whichPortrait labeled '#12.' below.
is of green or blue taffeta, as
the following figure shows.
Of the Complications Which
Sometimes Occur in This
Cure, etc.:
In this cure of the cataract, in both respects,
at times several dangerous accidents
befall the patient's eyes, causing great harm and
pain—such that the physician must
diligently apply remedies in time
to help at that very hour.
More depends on such complications than
on the greatest diligence in turning them aside,
even than couching the cataract itself,
and the evils are the following:
First Complication: Where the Cataract
Has Grown Fast [Adherent]
Where the cataract has grown fast in the eye, so that you
had to loosen it by force,
whence great danger arises—
come in time to prevent this and
use the following remedy:

Take [℞] egg-whites, no. 6; tormentil water [▽] 1 oz [℥j]; camphor [XXX]
½ drachm [ℨß]; mix the egg-white together as before, then
add the camphor [XXX] and mix therewith,
and apply with flax pledgets.
Note: when a cataract is grown fast,
you should always take 1 oz [℥j] tormentil water [▽]
and ½ drachm [ℨß] camphor [XXX], and apply it.

jured Eyes —

The 4th Complication: When Great
Pains Come Into the Eyes
—
This grievous and painful condition is
very common among patients, and often happens
that if one does not come to help in time, the
sight is spoiled and suffers great harm; for
it happens at times that from excessive headache
they quite lose their senses, become raving and
furious, so that one must bind them in chains
and fetters, or else from pain
must die, or their eyes burst
right out of their head; others who had such
pains for half a year, a whole year, and
a year and a half—for when such
pains take root, they are very hard
to drive away. These pains do not attack
continuously, but often only 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, 6, or 8 days, and stay away until
something stirs them.
Whence Such Pains
Come —
First, such pains are caused
by inexperienced physicians who
do not understand the art well and use unshaped
instruments, wherewith they tear the eyes,
so that the watery humor runs
out—sometimes even the vitreous humor—
so that the eyes suppurate internally,
whence such intolerable pains arise.
Secondly, such pains come when
one does not handle the puncture rightly and injures [the eye],
and in bandaging
it is negligently pressed too hard.
Thirdly, when cold and heat strike into the
eye before it is healed,
whence also great headaches follow.

It also happens indeed that even when a goodPage number '78' in upper-right corner.
oculist applies all diligence, yet it does not
go according to his wish as he would like;
yet such is not always the physician's fault,
but is often a punishment of God, and of
people's sins.
There are also other things which cause such pains:
such as severe coughing, vomiting, great
anger, fright, great fear and anxiety,
and sleeplessness, constipation of the stool
and urine [⊡], descending fluxes of the head, warm
weather in heat and drinking, looking too soon into fire
and air, and more such things—especially when
many a patient is obstinate or so coarse
that he will not use the prescribed things.

Aches of the Head —
First, for such patients it is necessary to

Take [℞] choice senna leaves, tamarinds, winter-cherry [Juden-]

as much again.

root ½ drachm [ℨß], zedoary ½ drachm [ℨß]; boil all in 1 lb [℔j] beer
as above; thereof use

[Epiphora] —
That in the cataract cure the eyes run with water

accustomed.
Secondly, it comes from the great heat and

Thirdly, it comes from great head and
eye pain, as was mentioned before. Such
running and dripping often lasts long; often

The Eighth Complication: When
Before the Eyes Everything Appears
Red, Green, Yellow, Blue, White, etc.
This condition happens quite often: when the
patient stands up and walks about, everything
he looks at appears to him to be of this or
that color.
If someone thinks everything is gray, then the
cause is that the cataract matter has divided in the eye,
or parted asunder, and
mixed among the aqueous humor, through
which the patients see as though
the cataract matter were [colored].
If, however, everything appears red, blue, yellow,
or green, the cause is that the aqueous humor
is mixed with blood, or
blood has settled in the conjunctiva.
If, however, it appears before the eyes as though
little gnats, flies, threads, cobwebs
were present, or as if looking through a net or a
sieve, this is also a sign that the cataract
matter has divided/fragmented in the eye.
Thereto use the following things:
If it is from blood, one should purge the patient
with flowers of cassia dissolved in fumitory water [▽]
and syrup, in the evening one hour
after eating, and in the morning
fast until noon. It is also very good for the
patient to be bled on the hand
or arm, and likewise have cupping-glasses set on
his neck and shoulders; thereto at meals also

one should take care of the head against thePage number '81' in upper-left corner; continues from p. 80 col. B l. 41.
heat.

The Tenth Complication: When
a Couched Cataract Rises Up
and Lays Itself Before [the Pupil] Again.
It happens at times that a couched
cataract moves upward again and places
itself again before the uvea, so that the person
is afterwards blind as before; and this
happens on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, or 8th day.
Such rising up, however, is caused
as follows:
First, the cause is that the cataract was not rightly
ripe, and was only scraped from the uvea
and not laid in its proper
place, but only pressed beneath the
pupil; when such cataracts are
young, they rise up again very soon.
Especially when the patient will not lie still,
when they must cough and retch,
suffer vomiting, or when they
do not lie still with the head, sit up, or
turn onto their side; very often it happens
to those who do not restrain themselves, or else
have no sense.
When, however, an oculist has rightly and well
worked the cataract, and without harming the eye
nor tearing the cataract matter, and the
patient has been cared for in the cure as is proper,
even if a cataract should immediately
rise again and lay itself forward, yet it has
no lasting harm; for I have often experienced thatFirst-person clinical observation by the practitioner.
such cataract matter gradually wastes away
and disappears, and the patient in the meantime,
without any other aid of medicine,
recovers his sight again—of which I could cite
many examples. When, however,
such matter does not disappear, and the patient
remains blind, he can after half a year
or a whole year be couched again.
When the cataract matter is torn or divided,
know that it is not soon to be couched again;
use now further as follows:

First, one should purge such patients
with panis laxativus, or with
species dia-turbith; after this set
vesicatoria behind his ears or on his
neck.
A Good Electuary for the
Re-Ascended Cataract —
Take [℞] skimmed honey ½ lb [℔ß]; eyebright flowers, lovage
herb, of each 1 drachm [ℨj]; valerian root, fennel
seed, wild thyme [?], of each 6 drachms [ℨvj]; make fine powder [ꝑll̵] and
mix with the honey; afterwards mix thereto
1 drachm [ℨj] white amber oil; stir until it grows cold.
Thereof the patient should morning and evening
always take the size of a nutmeg.
A Good Water for This
Complication —
Take [℞] eyebright flowers, valerian root, fennel
seed, rue, of each 2 oz [℥ij]; pound all, pour there-
on rose-water [▽] 1 lb [℔j]; let stand 6 days, then
distill in Balneo Mariae; put this water [▽] evening and morning
into the eyes, and lay it also with little cloths over
night upon the eyes.
Of Fistulae of the Eyes:
Fistula Lacrimalis —
Eye fistulae are very common, and are
frequently found, especially among children
who have survived smallpox [Blattern], and when
the same break out in the corner of the eye by the
nose, they cause a fistula.
It can also come from hot and salty
fluxes, which corrode the lacrimal bone in
the eye corner and make it ulcerous, so that
this little hole begins to suppurate and becomes a
fistula, so that the underlying
bone is attacked by the matter and becomes ulcerated or
carious, and in time eats away behind the

eye and in the meantimePage number '82' in upper-right corner.
draws very great evil after it. These fistulae
are poorly understood by many surgeons
and only taken for fluxes;
how one may recognize them is to be
seen from the following:
When one presses such a patient with
the finger in the large corner of the eye
by the nose, if it is a fistula,
there will appear in the eye a
little swelling or discharge—some-
times white and membranous matter comes forth,
in some so much that it runs over
the cheek and face downward, as
the following figure shows.
These fistulae have no other cure except
that one cuts them and afterwards burns with hot iron
[cautery]; sometimes they are cured even without incision
yet that rarely succeeds, and
only in young ones where it is still quite new and

yet even then it rarely succeeds. The surest cure is cutting and burning [cautery], as IPage number '83' in upper-left corner.
have cured many of them. The manner and way to cure the same is undertaken as follows.
First, purge the patient with good head pills; afterwards, if he is
plethoric and age permits, a vein may also be opened. When this has been done, prepare
everything belonging thereto: bandages, pledgets, plasters, compresses, styptics; then seat the
patient in an armchair, bind his hands thereto as the following figure shows.

Behind the patient there should also be someone who holds the patient's head; after this,
consider carefully whether the fistula is large or small, which you may tell beforehand from the
greater or lesser amount of matter; take then a thin, handy little knife
or a suitable lancet, and cut into the depth as far as you can reach down to
or close to the bone; and take great care that you do not injure the tear-sac/duct,
nor the corner angle of the eye, for from that a watering wound and weeping of the
eye would arise; therefore one must be very careful with the incision.

Way and Manner to Cure
the Eye Fistula, Namely
by Perforating or
Boring Through.
First, when you wish to cure a fistula of the eyes,
attend to it 3 or 4 days
before the incision and consider well
where the matter has its seat, and
what kind of matter it is, and where it
has its seat; for accordingly one must
direct or undertake the incision.
When this has happened and one sees
where most of the matter lies, one must
not let the matter out for 2 or 3 days,
so that the matter
gathers and fills the little cavity
and becomes puffed up, and thus the
incision can be performed more surely and
certainly.
Afterwards take a good healing/protective plaster
cut large enough to cover the eye alone,
and lay it over the closed eye;
one may also bandage the sound eye
so that the patient does not see, and the
better holds still; if one must cut on both eyes,
one should cover both eyes with the
plaster.
Afterwards the physician takes a good sharp
incision knife as I showed before,
and makes the cut deep down
to the bottom of the fistula; one should
take good care that one makes the cut
wide enough, so that afterwards
one can reach the bottom more easily.
The cut must be considered lengthwise
and not cut crosswise.

When the cut is made, lay a
prepared sponge tent therein, as large as
the wound can bear—the first time
not too large, for it swells with a
force apart and causes great
pain; let it remain therein 24 hours.
After the wound is well widened,
use 2 or 3 times the caustic things that I
described previously, so that that
slimy skin/sac is cleared out which lies
in the bottom of the fistula; when the dead
slough has cleaned away, use once
or twice more the sponge tents,
so that the wound is widened and
one may come the more easily to perforating
it.
Then seat the patient in an armchair
as the following figure shows [p. 88], with
the arms well bound, and with the following
instrument bore through the os cribrum [ethmoid/lacrimal bone].Label '#.o 6.' appears above the three bone drills.

Boring through is useful for nothing other than that an air/passage is made there, and

not only can no longer flow through the eye, but with empty moisture

First, of Smallpox Films

These films are called ungula ex pustulis,
smallpox film, or nail-film [pterygium/pannus], and come
most often to children from childhood
smallpox.
Secondly, such films are also seen in
adult people, from common ulcers
which settle upon the eyes; afterwards some films
grow and draw over the entire eye.
Thirdly, the cause is often only
a thick tough phlegm which descends from the head

into the eye, and there turns into a white
or gray film; some films also begin
at the large [inner] corner, others at the
small [outer] corner, others come from
above downward or from below upward, as
the following 2 figures show.
These films are still curable in the young,
if they have not stood too long; in the old
there is little or no hope to be made.

Eyes —
Burn films occur in those people
mostly from external causes, such as
when a fire-spark, a coal,
or flame and the like hot things spring into the
eyes, whereby the cornea is burned;
and they are called panni ex ambus-

or something flies into an eye,
and the same is not soon
brought out again. Such films
often cover the entire eye and spoil
sight greatly; and if one lets such films
lie and grow old, they are hard or
not at all curable.
The cure consists in this: that one
sets cupping-glasses on the temples, purges, and
behind the ears; all other medicines
need not be repeated here, since
they belong to another condition; yet it is
in the cure between burn films and
smallpox films a small difference.

Of Watery Films [Hydropic Pannus]
These watery films have their origin from
superfluous cold moisture which flows from
the brain and blood to the eyes
and swells both tunics, cornea and conjunctiva,
so that they swell up and
puff up, and become thick like a
piece of leather soaked in water [▽], and thereby the eyes
are robbed of sight and become blind.
Such films are also found when a watery
blister-skin of the eyelids occurs, which
incessantly rubs and pricks the eyelids,
causing the eyes continually to water
and drip, whence the said
cornea becomes thick and dull; and if
one lets such a condition stand too long,

it spoils; yet for the most part not beyond
help.

are remedied.

Of Blood and Flesh
Films [Pterygium] of the Eyes.
These blood and flesh films of the eyes are
called Sebel or panniculus carnosus; theySebel = Arabic sabel (pannus / vascular pterygium).
arise from blood and flesh, when
superfluous blood is the chief cause, because
the blood distends the veins until the tunics
press around and make such flesh grow,
which finally emerges out of the corners of the eyes
and covers over the conjunctiva and cornea.
Such films can also come
from striking, knocking, wounds, whereby the eye
is damaged, and the congealed blood
coagulates, whence a blood-film can grow.
At the beginning it is easy to help; as soon as it
turns into flesh and the eye is covered
therewith, the cure is laborious, difficult,
and dangerous. When, however, such
films come from fire and burning, there is
no hope at all to be made.
This cure is especially to be directed so that
one acts swiftly and in time, and
performs bloodletting and cupping right away,
and then makes use of the following things.

With these or similar medicinal remedies one should
persevere a while, for this cure does not let itself
be hurried; also often and many times
one cannot bring down such films with powders and waters,
but rather they must be removed by manual
cure and instrument.
Which is not only a great danger, but
also causes great pain;
and such a cure is only undertaken in extreme
necessity.
How, however, such a cure is undertaken
is to be seen from the following:
First, seat the patient in an armchair,
bind him by hands and feet, in
no high chair, but a low armchair, so
that it is convenient for you, as indeed
the following figure shows, so that
he can neither stir nor move
and cause harm during the operation.

When the patient is well bound in the said
manner, someone should stand behind him
who holds his head, and likewise another
at the side who opens his eyelids
and draws them apart. Afterwards take
a clean curved needle with a
flexible shaft and a slightly
curved tip, and thread a fine
silk thread therein; grasp the
fleshy film cleanly with the point
and pass the needle beneath it toward
the uvea and pupil; pierce through
the film cautiously, lest you pierce
through the cornea or conjunctiva
or come too close and injure them;
as the following figure clearly
shows the manner and form [p. 98, D].

Figure of the Flesh Film [Pterygium].Portrait labeled '.D.' below.
When now the beginning has been happily made,
take a small narrow little knife
which is very sharp and pointed, and grasp
the drawn-through silk thread with both
ends in your left hand, and draw the film
somewhat upward, and loosen it with the little knife
quite cautiously off, so that one neither
inflicts any harm on the eye nor cuts the
thread; yet it must be completely and wholly
detached, for if anything thereof
remained behind, it would easily
grow again and draw over the eye
anew.

Of the Gnat or
Fly Spots [Maculae] of the Eyes.
This defect is called gnat-spot
or fly-spot, for it appears
commonly upon the cornea, where it springs
of itself and shows almost the
size of a fly, making a spot
upon the pupil; often this dot is so small
and fine that one can scarcely see it
upon the pupil—yet small and fine as

it is, it nevertheless hinders sightPage number '99' in upper-left corner; continues from p. 98 col. B l. 35.
in such a way that the person sees as
if through a cobweb or thread.
This condition befalls old and young
people; this defect has its origin
from impure sharp humors
which from the blood or brain settle
into the eye tunics and cause this
defect. In other people it also happens at times
from smoky air or sharp wind, or when
a fly or dust flies into
the eye, which at first makes a thin
little cloud, which mostly recurs in
those who have weak/watery eyes, and
causes great harm to many.

Of the Evil and Long-Lasting
Eye Fluxes, Running,
Burning, and Weeping of the Eyes
The perpetual hot dripping and watering
of the eyes commonly comes from the head,
brain, and blood, or rather from
superfluous moisture of the brain, from
great pains and aches of the head.

These causes, however, are of two kinds,
namely hot and cold, which every [oculist]
will know how to distinguish;
therefore I will first treat of the hot eye
fluxes.
These hot eye fluxes have their first
origin from the brain, when the same is over-
burdened with hot blood and humor;
the eyes—and their vitreous and aqueous
humors—are quickly heated,
so that such humor with
great pain presses through the tunics of the
eyes, spoils them, and brings on
blindness.
So too come such hot fluxes from the
blood, namely when the
blood in the person grows too
abundant and heated, or is
inflamed by bile, whereby the eyes grow very
hot, runny, and red.
Above all, it is necessary that this patient
use a digestive, afterwards purge,
let blood, and use vesicatoria, and
therewith observe a good diet.

Of Cold Eye Fluxes,
Whence They Come, and How They
Are to Be Cured. .G.
The cold fluxes drip and run from the
eyes; [this] comes from superfluous cold mois=
ture of the brain. Secondly, from the weak=
ness of the head, when the same has taken on a cold
and great chilliness, a similar cold quality
to itself. Thirdly, from weak=
ness and debility of the brain and head, whereby
the eyes are very much weakened, and the
natural moisture is driven out,
whereupon then the running and dripping of the eyes
follows. The cure should well be started in the following
manner:

Of Old, Long-Last=Page number '106' in upper-right margin.
ing Evil Eye Fluxes.
.H.
Such long-lasting eye fluxes occur
often already in children, especially those
who previously had smallpox severely, whence mois=
ture remains, or those who in their
youth endured many headaches,
where often such fluxes continue into
old age.
Also such a flux comes [sometimes?] from
endemic/constitutional illnesses,
such as scurvy, French pox [syphilis], scabs, and the like.
How, however, such headaches, head
pains, and fluxes cause such eye disease
comes solely from the long
lasting afflux of the evil humors,
which do not consist solely in excess,
since nature drives everything into this
part and seeks to expel them through the ears
and reinforces and blocks these parts
and especially when it can run into the eyes.

107 thus accumulates and preserves the visual powerPage number '107' in upper-left margin; continues from p. 106 Col. B.
free, and to spoil such fluxes can be mighty.
How One Should Counter Such Fluxes,
Is to Be Understood as Follows.
The best help, of which I also have my own ex=
perience, is the cord [Schnüer], or seton [Setaceum], or
noose [Laqueum] called, which one draws through the skin
of the neck; and although to the patient
it seems frightening and hard, yet out of
necessity one must make a virtue, and of two evils
choose the better.
Before one resorts to the operation, one should
purge the patient 1 or 2 days beforehand.
—
Afterwards the physician should be provided with a
thereto belonging and suitable instrument, and
silk cord. The forceps and needle should be of
good steel, in such form and manner
as the present figure shows.

The needle should be pointed and sharp-edged in front; behind,
however, a fairly wide eye, so that a
cord the thickness of a feather quill can pass through.
The cord should be of red crimson silk,
twisted and threaded into the needle.
When now the needle, cord, and skin are seized,
and everything belonging thereto is ready, let
glowing coals be brought; lay the needle therein so that
it becomes quite fiery in front at the point. Then
seat the patient on a stool with his
back toward the window; draw with both
hands behind in the nape, between the neck
and [shoulders], as much skin as possible up into the
height, and grasp this pulled-up skin with
the forceps very firmly and strongly; screw then
the forceps very tightly shut, so that the skin cannot
slip out. Then take the glowing
needle and thrust it through the 2 holes of the iron
on the forceps, up to half the cord.
Unscrew then, let the forceps loose, and take
it away, and cut the cord off from the
needle; the cord one coats in front with
fresh butter, and afterwards make
at each end behind a knot.
This cord one draws afterwards daily half
back and forth; do this morning and evening
in such manner so the moisture can all the
more easily flow away and out.
It happens, however, sometimes that the holes
grow shut again with flesh, seeking to fill
up, so that not only the cord can with
great pain and difficulty be drawn,
but also the flux does not go and no
matter discharges, so that the head cannot
yet purge its fullness and get rid of the superfluous
moisture. Therefore,
the following salve will afterwards be exceedingly
precious and good, which applied to the
cord removes the excess
newly grown flesh in the wound
and bites it away again and clears it out of the way.
Draw it thus on the cord,
pulling so much through that the salve
is brought into the entire wound; and
this one does as often and as many times until
the cord moves more easily again and the
flux has its course and flow again.

Figure of How the Cord Should Be
Placed in the Neck
.K.
As soon as all this has happened and the cord
has been passed through, anoint around
with warm rose oil to soothe the pain
and prevent other inflammation.
Thereupon lay the diapalma plaster and
bind with a little compress therein, and band=
age as is fitting, and leave it thus until
tomorrow, the second day. On the second day draw
the cord halfway, well and cleanly
anointing with fresh butter, and afterwards
always with a common digestive
salve, so that it draws matter especially
and promotes the flux.

Or When an Eye Is Stabbed
[Pierced].
It happens oftentimes that an eye is
stabbed with a knife, scissors, wood,
nails, or other things. Such happens
oftentimes among children who like to play with
knives, or also with
brawling or falling in their quarrels, and
however it happens, such stabs or cuts are very
dangerous, especially when the stab goes deep
penetrating into the eye, cornea, uvea, and
injures other parts; so especially is it
grave and dangerous when the humors are
injured and even run out, and when
the crystalline humor—which is the cause
of sight—is lost, then it is all over.

Of Diminution of Sight,
Debility, Dimness, and
Cloudiness of the Eyes.
The foremost cause of a weak
and dim sight is old age, and the
departed youth. It is an old prov=
erb: in old churches one finds
dark windows; therefore when a
person grows old, not only does the
sight decrease, but also all strengths out of the
limbs; yet one still finds very old people
who have a clear and sharp sight,
as good as a young person; conversely one finds
also many young people who have a weak,
dim sight.
A weak sight also arises from ex=
cessive lingering phlegm, such as garlic,
peas, lentils, porridge, baked foods,
dark meat, fish, old cheese; these and similar
things make coarse vapors and fumes, which
rise into the head and settle in the eyes,
and hinder the vital spirits in
their perfect course; therefrom follows
a sharp dimness and debility of the eyes.
Again, a dim sight can come
from thick, tough phlegm which lies
by the brain on the optic nerve
[nervus opticus], or on the veins of the eyes,

or the vitreous or albugineous humor,
mixing and making the same cloudy, whereby the
sight is hindered and becomes dim.
A weak sight also comes from much
weeping and sadness, as also from looking too much
into fire and snow, from much waking, and
when one reads much small writing by night
or writes, from much bloodletting,
from old frost and [?], and other
causes more.
.M.
One finds three kinds of eyes: black, grey,
and blue. The black are the strongest and
sharpest; the blue the weakest, yet
besides the loveliest; the grey are
the most nimble and of moderate strength. It
is also a difference between the large
eyes and small eyes: the large and prominent eyes
are, because they protrude, not as
strong; the small eyes, however, are much
sharper and more enduring.
When, however, one wants to help
some weak, dim, and clouded eyes,

full of all kinds of the very best, most precious

Stinging and Pressing of the Eyes
The stinging and pressing of the eyes has its cause
from superfluous hot moisture, which settles in the
membranes of the conjunctiva,
so that it often seems to the person no differently than if he had
sand in the eyes.
Also such a sensation can be caused
by raised little blisters in the eyes.
Also this pressing and stinging can come
from too much blood in the little veins

of the eyes, filling the same too much.
This ailment one should prevent in time,
for sometimes great pain arises therefrom.
One should, however, first consider from which
cause it comes: if it comes from super=
fluous moisture, then it is necessary to
purge; if it comes from excess of blood,
then one must let blood by vein and cupping.

Of the Misdirected Hairs of the Eyelids, which Injure and Offend the Eyeball.
This condition is a harsh and grievous evil, which deprives countless people of their sight; for these little hairs turn/move themselves a little [inward], as if continuing without ceasing day and night, swelling and stiffening, so that the eye is brought to a continual watering, such that afterwards the tunica cornea becomes thick and dark from the incessant pokes, and is ruined in such a way that the patient must lose his sight entirely, and even if some slight glimmer of vision is preserved, nothing worse can befall such eyes.
The cause of this condition is a coarse melancholic blood, which follows the moisture of the eyes, and through the pores of the eyes, with its sweating out, finally settles itself commonly on the upper eyelids, and pricks into the eyes and presses upon them from above, so that the hair grows somewhat crooked/inward. Likewise it comes from the coarse superfluous humors, which settle themselves in a glassy/glistening form on the outer parts of those same eyelids, so that from the inflammation/outbreak they only grow out toward the eyeball.
Which wicked hairs [are] to be cured in the manner recounted, as follows. [49]

The First Cure of the Wicked Hairs of the Eyes.
First, an ancient learned authority has held that one should purge the head of superfluous moisture, draw it off and clear it; [using] fennel [?] or pills, whichever the patient can most commendably take.
A Good Purgative Powder.
Take: fine sugar, 1.5 oz.; choice senna leaves, 2 oz.; diagridium [scammony], turbith, gum esula [spurge], prepared [?], cloves, of each 1 dram; a little ginger. Make a fine powder, mix, for a dose of 1 dram.
After this, it is necessary to let [blood from] the cephalic vein on the arm or on the hand, and to have cupping glasses placed on the neck and shoulders, so that his blood is drawn away and diverted from the eyes.
Likewise, vesicatories [blistering plasters] behind the ears are very useful, so that the wicked moisture is taken away from the eyes and out of the head. Then it is necessary to pull out the hairs completely with suitable instruments; for even if there are only 2, 3, 5, or 6 little hairs, one should remove them by pulling them out, and see with diligence that one brings them out together with the root. When this has been done, use the following powder.
Powder for the Plucked-Out Hairs.
Take: dried caraway/cumin seed, fleabane [?], XX, O, ⊡, of each a sufficient quantity; pound/roast them together in a small pan until they become nice, white, and hard, then make a fine [powder]. Dip this with a little thread [or feather] into the hair follicles, and let the patient keep the eye closed for half an hour. With this powder I have helped many people.
Another.
Take: chondrilla juice, 0.5 oz.; mastic, 2 oz.; +, O, white [?], of each 1 dram; pound everything together and smear it into the follicles.

[Rubric:] The third cure is to cut away the hairs together with the flesh.
When everything is prepared for this, seat the patient on a chair, bind him in all [respects ...] as is shown in the figure [...], so that he does not reach in between with his hands or untie himself. Thereafter take a surgical suture needle (Heftnadel) threaded with a red [...] silk thread; thereafter take a suture cannula (Heftröhrlein), gently lift the eyelid, and pierce it with the suture needle. Pull the thread through and cut it off so that it hangs a finger's length at both ends, as the following figure clearly shows you. Such piercing should be done 3 times on each eyelid, or 4 times; then grasp all 3 or 4 threads in one hand and draw the eyelid evenly forward. Hold it thus evenly elevated, and with the other hand take the scissors and cut evenly behind the thread from one corner to the other, and take great care that you do not cut outside the corner of the eye-angles and leave no hair-stump standing; and the eyelid should be cut away evenly up to the width of 2 knife-backs, so that the hair roots are removed everywhere, and it is properly done thereafter.

Of the trembling and twitching
of the eyelids.
There are people found who with the eye=
lids quiver and tremble, some only at times,
some however continuously, and it is not possible for them
to hold them still. For when such trembling
is hereditary, there is no hope of help to be
had; when, however, it comes only at times
and passes away again, this comes solely from
winds and vapors; these can still be
healed and cured.
The third kind, however, is like a convulsion,'Confulsion' = Convulsion.
for it commonly draws the eyelid toward
the outermost corner. The cause, however, is when
the blood presses closely and wants to go to the eyes
by crowding, or through a vein or other [passage],
or bleeds toward the nose.
Often it can come from cold rheums settling upon these
little muscles, which also otherwise have not
been cooled.
It can also come from anger and fear.
The help consists in this, that one first uses good
head pills, and they be taken early in the morning;
such pills may be used once every 14 days.

Of the Tertian (Three-Day) FeverLarge rubricated heading in red ink.
Spuria or BastardRed ink.
Febris Tertiana Notha, or Spuria, or Bastard,
comes from mixed and diverse moistures,
especially from pituita (phlegm) with the
predominance/mixture of bile and putrefaction; it comes with
chills, and readily in spring. When this putrid
humor is in the great veins and near the heart,
there comes from it a tertiana continua
duplicata; afterwards it turns into a
malignancy and kills the person. Where,
however, the putrefaction is around the liver, spleen, or
mesenteric veins, it becomes a simple tertian,
or only continua. This appears or lasts longer
than the true tertian, and commonly exceeds
the term, that is, the 7th paroxysm;
it even extends itself up to the 40th day.
And when the spleen is much involved therewith,
it can last 6 months or more. When it ceases
on the second day, one is out of danger;
if it becomes continua therefrom, it is unto death.

Fever.Red rubric.
It also happens in this fever that
pregnant women lose their fruit (miscarry) before term;
and even if they carry until full term, they
give birth to weak, sickly children, which either
soon die, or are very delicate and burdened with severe
illness, and afterwards commonly die.
Often the children in the mother's womb [die], and often leave
[danger] very swiftly around them, and it kills them very
soon. Therefore pregnant women should
take good care to guard and protect themselves
in good time. Therefore one need not
have any scruple herein against [giving]
medicine or ...; one can purge pregnant
women and let blood if necessity
requires it, as the matter indicates, from the fourth
month until the seventh; but what is
under [four] or in older [later] time, one should be very cautious.
One should also not worry, for one must [treat] pregnant
women's medicines not too roughly or too strongly; one

Of Coughing.Large red ink heading
Coughing is a necessary/natural movement of the lung,
which is promoted by the air and the motive power of the little
muscles, when [something] is contrary or
harmful to the lung, so that the cough may cast out and
cleanse the foam/phlegm, which casts out the superfluity of impure
watery, viscous matter from the lung. And
it arises firstly not only around the air on account of the
throat, but also in the windpipes of the lung, when
the same are clogged with phlegm, obstructed, and filled with viscous matter,
and such phlegm-foam commonly trickles down from the head
onto the chest; for these reasons, coughs can
cause [?] creeping moisture of the chest. Often
coughing comes from the rising of vapors from the liver,
stomach, spleen, and womb, which enters the little windpipes of the
lung; and when the lung has small ulcers,
from this comes the retention of air, for
from retention [comes] a sudden death, so that he dies suffocated
[and] lies dead.
When a cough comes from a sharp head-flux,
it attacks the lung and makes an ulcer in it,
or settles [?] in the lung.

one can, after long strong coughing in sleep, with

Of Great Thirst.
Great thirst often comes from the hot
stomach. Finally from great inflammation of the liver
and the bile. Or when in the stomach much salted
bile and phlegm lies, or much sharp pituita, or

when an inflammation arises in the stomach. For [there] is a lack and want of moisture,
or when very many salted or spiced foods are eaten,
or strong heating wines are drunk. Thus there is often great thirst in severe
hot fevers, in sciatica, dropsy, also in the inflammation of the
lungs and of the heart. Whoever [has a] hot [throat/passage?], thus the stomach can come to evil.

Of Heart Palpitation and Trembling
Heart palpitation comes from various causes, such as evil
or poisoned vapors from the spleen [or] womb, which [rise] into the
heart, stinging, injuring, heating and tormenting the heart. It can
also come from too much [dryness?] or moisture. It comes
also for the most part from an intemperate liver, for
the same cannot make good blood, which would help
the heart; thus the heart has no good nourishment therefrom. Or else
the blood is too abundant or hot, or much too thick. It comes

the injured [parts] etc. It can also come from fright, anger, fear, ingested poison, evil
lack of appetite, belly-ache(?), and the like. Those who in youth often
get heart palpitations do not grow old, for fainting often follows upon it. If you
find it altogether, the heart suffers then from the bile, and from the [?] in the whole body.

The ulcer or aposteme in
the breast is a gathered
pus between the lung and the pleura (rib-membrane), which
must be coughed out with coughing. This one
recognizes when the patient feels on one side of the
breast a heaviness or some pain
when the breath is short, which sometimes is with a
little fever, sometimes without fever, and when [the]
pus is long retained, and the feet swell,
and every night a strong sweat breaks out on him.
A gentle continuous fever shows itself in him, more
by night than by day, alongside a continual
cough. One notices that the
pus falls from one place to another when
one turns from one side to the other.
At the end the cheeks become red, and the
eyes deep [sunken].

Asthma,
or shortness of breath.
This disease comes from obstruction of the
windpipes, which draw the breath in and out
and carry it in and out; when thus the tubes
are obstructed, they cannot perform their office
and relieve it lighter and easier. This
bad moisture (phlegm) comes sometimes from the head
through the nerves into the lung, and settles in
all the little tubes of the lung, wherein it
corrupts and greatly harms, or causes to ferment,
which causes much wind in the lung, which checks the
breath, causing a long hoarse wheezing and rasping
with a sensation as if they would suffocate.
This disease is great or small according to
whether the matter is much or little, even though
this disease often comes from other organs,
such as stomach, womb, spleen; therefore always
one should examine the sick person, so that
one may recognize whence the condition has its origin.

On the Distinction of the BloodRed-ink rubric
First, the substance of the blood is observed.
This blood is phlegmatic, which flows slowly, which
sticks between the fingers, and is gluey.
The blood which is of viscous and clotted blood, and slowly
runs, has many defects.
This blood is a cause of obstruction and other
diseases, which runs slowly to the outflow, the same
is hard and very thick.
Which blood is cold, and yet not clotted or hard
becomes, the same is putrid and watery.
The blood which one touches and immediately comes
apart and disintegrates, this blood is putrid.
When much water, bile-yellow, swims upon the blood,
that indicates a weak liver, or great foulness
in the obstructed kidney.
When some foam swims on top, and not from the [?]
scarcely easily disappears, it indicates the heat of the
putrid humour. The colour [is] altered beforehand.Crossed-out word after 'farb'
The red foam [indicates] the heat and burning of the
blood. The gold-yellow foam signifies the bile,
the white [signifies] the phlegm; the blue [signifies] the melan-
cholic humour.
When above in the blood swims a moisture
like a spider's web, this, when the body is moist,
is [thereafter], becomes [a sign] that the blood is inclined to
putrefaction. If however the body becomes lean, and
it indicates that the body is weakened and wastes away.
When one lets blood, and the first little glass is fair, but
the last is bad, then it is a sign that still much
impure blood is in the body.
Young children should not be bled before 14 years [of age],
because the same [diseases] which arise from blood
can very easily be quenched with other remedies.
Early bloodletting in youth is harmful, for thereby
the vital spirits are exhausted, and the body weakened,
and the whole body thereby cooled. Therefore
frequent bloodletting shortens life before its time,

Concerning Melancholy and BloodRubricated major heading
Purification, I come to the Spleen'sRubricated major heading
Illness, for Relief.Rubricated major heading
Between the spleen and liver, [regarding] their illnesses,
there is no small difference in consideration, for one
mixes the composition, since the recipes and medicines
—for the most part, those which one uses for the liver—
are also good for the spleen. When one,
however, considers the cause of both illnesses, then
the medicine [becomes] notable: thus, if the medicine
is good and a [principal] medicine, thus it can be all
the [same] medicine.
The cause, however, consists in this, namely in an
obstruction and sliminess/mucus accumulation; namely, when the
vessel between the liver and spleen, behind the stomach,
becomes obstructed and clogged with slime, whereby the
spleen is brought into an illness, and
some of the blood, full of slime and raw humors,
cannot flow through the portal vein to the liver,
but rather, contrary to nature, the blood [turns]
more toward the spleen, distending the spleen,
making gross black humors, [which] remain and
spoil in the spleen; from which great pains and
long-lasting melancholic illnesses flow forth.
It is the spleen's proper office that it
draws the melancholic humor to itself, which
is sent to it from the liver, which
is the liver's [superfluous/feculent] essential part. When,
however, such [humor] is too thick and slimy, it remains
stuck between liver and spleen, as above

Colic comes from four causes.
Firstly, from tough, slimy matter, which so
is cold, and has an appearance as if it
came into the stomach, and comes into the small intestine,
and when these with all the same winds are accom-
panied, then they cause great bitter
pressing pains. More so when in the bowel
colon it comes, can their essence in such
way recover and be softened with passion
accessing thus more end as it would have
out of ... belly-bladders blacken/pain.

according as the matter is much or
little, as long as the time holds out so that
it cannot pass forth.
It can thus come from a hot cause
when the matter is bilious, and in the heat thick
thin comes, then it gives stabbing pains, however
especially in the wind mixed with the bile,
sometimes however it is mixed, the
bile with phlegm and wind.
Thus the griping can come alone from winds
as well as from the constipation of the body.
when the excrements in the intestines dry up

How one can recognize from what
causes the pain may be.
When it is from a cold cause. Namely
the thick, raw phlegm, then the pains
are around the kidneys and in the flanks, now
on one, now on the other side, often
toward the stomach and liver. Sometimes there is
the urine [⊡] white, sometimes turbid and thick/grittyAlchemical/medical symbol ⊡ (square with dot) used here for urine or salt
comes from coldness. There are fevers and
heat and thirst therewith. Further, no stool
often, and great stabbing, tearing pains;
for the bile gnaws and frets the intestines
dark from the cold black [bile]. Also often
the matter even goes out by the mouth
because it has a retention in the intestines
congested; in these the pains awaken,
the pulse is hard and small, and when
feverishness joins it, then the
sick person dies.
When it comes from winds, then is
the belly around the navel distended and puffed
up.
When it however from a constipated body
comes, one can just from the patient
learn it.
It also comes from suffering of the womb,
especially when one soon after birth
has taken medicine, and the body/ligaments

offends [ligamenta] with sharp drinks
of medicine.
Cure in the cold cause.
When the matter is in the large intestine colon,
then proceed carefully, so that one does not
slip out nor make it smaller. Examine the
patient very closely, before you small
ruptures can choose, as if no
volvulus, or cold gangrene in the intestines
can arise; rather begin with gentle
clysters, for before the passage is open,
give medicine by the mouth [only cautiously], for
if one gives medicine from above at the beginning,
one drives the matter forward into the intestines
and if it cannot pass forth, then one makes
the symptoms greater and worse.
When the pains are from a cold cause,
then use none at all, too hot
things, such as castoreum oil, euphorbium oil,
pepper and the like, for they resolve
too strongly, and when nature cannot
bring it forth, then it makes only greater
pains; rather one should give temperate and
mild things, now one, now the other,
and when it strikes in, to give, so
that nature can perform its work.
The clysters can be given first,
for that is more effective thereto.

This disease comes from the bile when it
overflows, which goes over the whole body
and is drawn into the blood; then there becomes
also the whole body yellow; it comes from the
obstructed liver and spleen, and from the black [bile].

struction of the liver is, so one should before all
things dissolve the obstruction, as well as
draw out a bilious matter.

Ascites, the third Anasarca.
Ascites is the second kind of dropsy;
this takes hold of the veins that
are in this manner. Ascites, this sickness,
begins at the feet to swell and
so continues onward until the belly and feet become
completely large and full of water, and especially
the watery fluxes, for it comes from
a soft [watery] matter which follows between the
peritoneum, with a part thin [mucous/serous],
yet the water is more than wind.

of dropsy; in this sickness the person
swells over the whole body, and it comes from a
cold, watery liver, which instead of
blood makes water, and mixes itself with the blood

and if one does not attend to it in time,
the water sinks into the belly and
becomes Ascites therefrom.
Tympanites, Wind-Dropsy
This sickness comes from wind accompanied by little
water; in this sickness the
belly alone swells up large, and when one
taps or strikes upon it with the fingers,
it gives a sound that rings clear like a
broken drum. With this swelling indeed
also the feet [swell], yet it is not so great as
with Ascites; thus the belly begins to
swell up large, round, and hard, and otherwise
with all [this], other limbs in the body
waste away thereby, and the feet become thin.
All these sicknesses come from the
principal or chief organs, namely
spleen and liver, which do not perform their office
rightly and well; if one considers the beginning,
the first originator and first cause
is the stomach, then the liver, and thereafter the
spleen. Now when the stomach is weak and

chilled, one may [harm] the stomach from heat or
cold, and [it is] the first cause of all illnesses,
to which one looks. In the stomach is
and is performed the first digestion. When
this is not well and good and thorough,
it remains raw, coarse, watery, and
mucous; which, when it enters the mesenteric
veins near the spleen and liver, makes the same
[faulty]; when then the blood is made therefrom,
a poor, coarse, and mucous
blood is formed, from which then
such an illness can easily arise.
Thus not only spleen and liver, but
also the stomach is a beginning of dropsy.

Yet it is thus to be known that not every pus
in their semen signifies a kidney abscess.
For it may well be that the pus settles in its own
place, and otherwise ulceration draws into the flux-
vessels, and is driven by nature to the
kidneys and passes forth with the urine.
When the pus comes out only after the
emitted semen, it is rather an
indication of a bladder ulcer. But if
the pus comes before the urine, then the gland-
ulae prostatae and remaining seminal vessels are
afflicted with an ulcer.
But if the kidney abscess comes with pus, then
it boils forth; thus much pus comes mixed with
the urine. The semen will initially appear
white, but soon the pus will settle
down and be turbid, while the remaining urine
will appear fairly natural.
If, however, the abscess is severe from a
softness/moisture, which has completely torn open
the little vessels and semen, then the semen will
likewise be extinguished in color, above the pus
which soon settles to the bottom, having a
different consistency, and swims on the color
as if fine ashes lay at the bottom.
All these abscesses are very dangerous, yet
that which comes from inflammation is
more easily and quickly cured than that which
comes from sand and stone. In this abscess
the whole body often wastes away and consumes itself
little by little.

The dissolved pearls are closely akin to an aurum potabile,
for they preserve the body in good health.
They drive away indisposition. In particular,
they prevent falling sickness, vertigo, and apoplexy.
sweat, and other ailments of the brain. It is also a

heart palpitations, and other illnesses of the heart
in all hot fevers. It is a splendid remedy
for those who are failing or beginning to weaken; it is
a refreshing medicine and nothing better can
be found than the pearl.

the use of the stag's heart-bone (Hirschkreuzel)Rubricated heading in red ink
The bones or crosses from the stag's heart
are very much and highly esteemed in medicine.
One buys very little of it in the apothecaries for
a thaler, and they are commonly mixed among
heart-strengthening medicines. These little bones,
however, are very rarely to be obtained from the stag,
and yet they are often sold by the hundred
at a time; and the deception consists
in this: I tell you that this or
similar little bone or cross every old ox has,
and you get this from the butcher. Cut
the heart of the ox, and you will find above at the
crown this little bone. Although it is from the ox
and not from the stag, it has the very same
power and efficacy as the stag's heart-bone.
Many hundreds of them are sold in the city
all in place of the stag's heart-bone, and are

of the stag's heart-bone not otherwise considered or declared.
Thus you can very easily come by this little bone
which you have needed in medicine.

How one should boil good soapRubricated heading in red ink
in 3 or 4 hours.Rubricated heading in red ink
At the first boiling, the art is solely to know
the knack, for some boil a whole
day at it and always make grease and no
soap; whereas white and pure soap can by some
be well produced in 3 or at most 4 hours
of boiling. For this, one uses this
way and manner.
Take a load of quite fresh ashes that is still
whole in lumps; three loads of good fresh
ashes cleanly sifted, put the ashes on the floor
cleanly together. Then stir the ashes a
little apart, so that one lays in the
middle the whole load of lime/ashes. Afterwards one sprinkles
until the lime, sprinkled with fresh water,Contains symbol ▽ (water)
completely breaks up and crumbles. And when it is fully
crumbled, one throws it quickly
over it in the form of a grave-mound, and beats
it with a high shovel and smooths it; let it thus
lie a quarter hour or an hour and a half; afterwards
one cuts a little and lifts it from the place
little by little in a certain way, whereby
the ashes and lime are well mixed together,
and afterwards forms a mound again as
before, and beats it down again well with the shovel;
let it lie again a full quarter
of an hour; work it down again with the hoe.
Afterwards it is poured into the lye-tub
in the following way: one takes a large
tub, makes a strong cross inside,
as wide as the tub is; the cross must rest on

432Boxed page number in top-left corner
wood finely ... and so high that
over the cross in the tub 4 or 5-fold cross
splints are placed; on the cross one lays a strainer
beaten from willow/wood and bored with holes.
The space or opening should be so
large that the ashes have plenty of room therein,
so that one may more easily proceed with pouring on.
On the bottom lay straw, so that
the ashes do not run through too suddenly. But if one lays
hay instead of it on the bottom, then
the lye becomes greenish. Afterwards lay half
of the ashes on, and tamp it with the hoe, yet so
that one can bore a little hole through with a finger.
Afterwards lay the other half
of the ashes thereon, and tamp again up
and down as above. Afterwards lay on top of the
ashes a bundle of straw, onto which one pours all
along, and further as the wood requires, so that
it seeps in quite gently and gently drips
through; thus one must take special care in pouring on,
so that the ashes
do not stand soft on top, until one
thinks one has enough lye. Afterwards
one takes a high kettle of lye and
measures 75 pounds, or tallow and clarified fat
1 ounce; puts it into the kettle and lets it gentlyContains apothecary symbol ℥i (1 ounce)
boil for a good hour long; afterwards pours
a scoop of lye therein again and pours,
lets it boil again for an hour. Note well: markNB: written in red ink
this well, that it is not good that one
boil strongly, but quite slowly and stir
about, so that one prevents it from boiling over.
If one were to make so great a fire that it
boils right over, then all would be spoiled. One must
make the fire so small that it only
remains boiling in a small simmer
and does not boil over everywhere.
Now when it has boiled 2 hours, one tests
it by rubbing salt/gold therein, green + or 2 parts,Contains symbols ☉, +, ℞ij
lets it boil thus for another half hour. For if
one still has a good leftover lye,
one can pour another half-pail full
in, when the salt/gold is therein, and proceedContains symbol ☉
without putting the lye away and drying

boiling, and straining it in through a colander.
When it is then fully boiled with the salt/gold and thusContains symbol ☉
thickened so that the lye around it
turns into a trough. Afterwards one takes a
small tub as large as one
wants to have the soap, and lays a half
damp linen cloth through it and lays
old ... therein, and with a scoop
one skims the soap off the top and pours
it into the little molds or tubs, and with a
paddle/scoop presses it so that it settles well
into the corners so that the lye still
comes out well. When one has poured all the soap
out, one drains the lye into the bucket
and then takes off the remaining separated soap;
the shape/thickness of the soap one can
make medium-sized as one wishes.
When one is at work making the lye,
one should not leave the lye in the
tub or in a pail, but cover it,
otherwise within an hour its strength
evaporates and the best power is gone.
One should also make no more lye than one
intends to use, and if it then goes
that is again a pity/loss. AndContains symbol ┼
so that one may recognize whether the lye is good,
one takes a fresh egg and lays it in
the lye; if the egg floats on top,
the lye is good; but if it falls to the bottom
and stays lying there, then the lye is too weak.
When one takes the soap out of the molds,
one trims it on top and makes
wider pieces out of it, and lays it in
the air so that it dries out gently
and is then ready to be used.
One must always see to it that when one
makes the lye, one has good fresh ashes
that are not very old or have lain in a damp
place for a long time and are half spoiled; for
the ashes one uses for this work,
one keeps the ashes in an airy place
stored.

Of the Ulcers and Fistula inRubricated heading in red ink
the Anus.Rubricated heading in red ink
These ulcers and fistulas commonly come from
the hemorrhoids, whose blood is mixed with other evil
humors, and finally is brought into an eruption,
so that from the same ulcer
it progresses until a fistula forms. Some of these fistulas are
deep or not; some reach up beyond the
rectum below the sphincter, while others
go back and forth with their channels, while others
go upwards toward the bladder, as happens
in men. The fistulas long retain the filth
because of the excrement and impurity that
comes thither, and also the expulsive force which sends such
evil humor into this place. One
must therefore often use the speculum
ani, so that one can look inside, so that one
knows where and how one should apply the medicine,
since from the ulcers the fistula
arises; so I will first speak of the ulcers
and afterwards of the fistula.

What remedies are usedRubricated heading in red ink
for the ulcers in the anus.Rubricated heading in red ink

Test the Precipitate
Take 1 grain, put it on a glowing coal and
blow gently on it. If it does not all go up in smoke
it is not pure, but do not smell it
must [stay]. If it remains on the coal, and changes
its color into gold, then it is good.

The cramp is a very evil and terrible,
also dangerous condition. It is a disease
of the nerves and muscles, a tension and drawing
with great pains.
Of the cramp there are three kinds: one
the true cramp or convulsion; the second
a convulsive movement, which goes back and forth
into a limb and goes away again; but the
true cramp is a continually lasting drawing and
tensing. The cramp comes from ...
blows, from too much evacuation, or too
great repletion. However, this cramp
disease is divided into 4 parts: one cramp that
draws the person with all force forward
and so strongly that he draws the head down to the knees;
the second is that it draws the head back-
ward in the neck and spine; indeed it draws
and locks in some the mouth so strongly together that
one cannot even with strong iron screws
bring it apart; the third kind is that the
muscles and nerves, front and back, with all force
pull equally, so that the person especially
cannot bend forward and leaves the body straight; the fourth
way is when a cramp attacks someone in a
jaw [?] and hands, arm.
The cramp from superfluous evacuation, as too
much purging, too much bleeding, it is always more danger-
ous than that which comes from superfluous repletion;
the cause of repletion comes from retention
of the hemorrhoidal vein, suppressed menses, superfluity of bloodContains alchemical/astronomical symbol ♀ (Venus/menses)
and the like; it is ... often in

Of fistulas in generalRubricated heading in red ink, positioned directly below the framed illustration
First of all, it is necessary for a physician
that he carefully explores with the probe the depth,
width, and corners of the fistula; if it however has more
than one passage, which one with the instru-
ment could not see, so one should with a
small probe pay attention to draw the same out again,
so one should then with swelling or tent dilators (Stellmeißel)
begin to widen the openings, so that
one may with the instrument all the more easily
reach inside.
The best and shortest way of all is that one
treats the fistula with cutting or cauterization (caustics),
for it is certain where one is cutting on account of
the danger of the great veins and nerves, which often
hinder the physician, so that one cannot
continue the cure as needed. For if
one must with the tent dilator alone widen
the width, it proceeds very slowly.
It is also not only a lengthy treatment, that
one delays oneself so long; thus it brings nothing,
nor anything else either. For in many a fistula there is
not just one hole, in some however there are found
many crooked canals and passages, 2, 3, 4, and
often even more; thus it is possible that one to all

Diarrhea comes from various
causes. First, when the children want the teeth
to come forth. 2, when the wet-nurse [feeds] the child with
warmth and fills it too much. 3, when
the milk is sharp and salty, so that when
the expulsive power runs too much,
and pushes out more than it should
be.
To recognize these fluxes, from whatever cause
it may ever be, one should not
stop it immediately, rather let it go for a while; for
even those same fluxes themselves serve for the nourishment
and strength of the child, which one should take careDittography of 'des'
how this is stilled. When such
flux is not strong or bloody and bile runs with it,
one should not stop it too soon, for such
diarrhea often serves for a cleansing of the
body.

Of Fevers in Young Children.Rubricated heading in red ink
Children are often attacked by fever, and
especially when their teeth are pushing through; since
however from a putrid, purulent, and
sharp matter it arises, and if one does not then
provide help, the children contract consumption and
die.
When the child is still small, one must keep the
wet-nurse in a good diet, of veal
and fresh meat. Her drink should be barley-water;
wine she should avoid completely, but
eat of cooling juice, or
drink other cooling distilled [waters] and thin broth.
And if it is necessary that the
wet-nurse purge, one should purge her with a
purgative such as manna and cassia.
The wet-nurse should not give the breast to the child
again until she has
ceased to purge.

For the hiccuping/sobbing of children.Rubricated heading in red ink
Hiccuping is an evil stomach condition
and is caused by the emptiness of the stomach
mouth, or from cold moisture that is in the stomach,
such as from cold air when the children become
too chilled, as in chewing/crying etc.
Sometimes it comes also from the rising vapor
of bile into the stomach.
It is, however, very common among children that it
comes from overfilling of the stomach; then
one finds the wet-nurse gluttonous; good counsel
is to give wine to drink and let her
refresh, so that she may not cause the children
more harm than benefit.

Children are easily attacked by this sickness
because they have moist brains.
Thus also all their limbs are still weak and
frail; therefore very many children are subject to this
affliction.
To some children, however, the falling sickness is
congenital, so that they are afflicted with it when they
are born into the world; to whomsoever it is
congenital, health can scarcely be
restored. If a child is conceived
when the woman is in her monthly
purification (menstruation), these children are commonly
prone to epilepsy, and with consumption,Continues at top of Right Column

because this impurity has penetrated too much into theContinues from bottom of Left Column

When a child [inherits] such a condition from a
mother's womb and afterwards from the same
does not break free, and it is begotten of old and sickly
parents, and all experience shows
in some it is painful to hear,
and even if physicians are consulted, the
illness is stubborn and difficult.
When a boy is attacked by this illness
in youth, and he is
not freed from it until his
beard begins to grow, and if he is not cured by
his 25th year, then there is
no hope thereafter.
And if a girl contracts it in youth
and until the time of her monthly purification
is not freed from it, then she must all her
life long be plagued with it.

The female sex is, besides other
common illnesses, subjected to many
others from which men are free;
for there are few illnesses
found among men, where the
womb is not most involved therein, and the one
obscures the other illness so much
that one often cannot here
believe or discern whence
their illness has its origin.
As for what concerns chlorosis, it has
its cause from a cold obstruction,
yet not entirely outside the womb, in
292Pencil foliation in bottom left margin

644Boxed page number in red ink at top right
the stomach, outside the stomach in the mesentery,
in the uterine veins, also in the liver; in
sum, it is a pure obstruction in the body.
Which obstruction is a cause that the
humors in the blood cannot have their natural course
and flow; thereupon follows an alteration
of the color in the face; the red
cheeks fade, the face becomes quite pale,
somewhat yellowish, blackish, and
languid-looking. They would rather eat
chalk, coals, or earth, and cannot
leave off; they are faint in the whole body
and beaten down; when they climb a staircase
or a small hill, they do not have
sufficient breath; the heart leaps and
beats in them; in their sleep some
are startled in such a way that every moment
they feel as if they might collapse from it.
They love to sleep by the hearth, sit near
as they wish to stir and walk about in the house,
and like to lie in the shade
long into the day, because of faintness
of the body. Although their heart rather
tends toward the vapor of this illness,
they do not recover enough to walk.

or less, according as the obstruction
is great or small.

On Fluor Albus (the white flux)Rubricated heading in red ink framed by horizontal red double rules above and below; contains alchemical symbol ☿/♀ and Fl ligature
This affliction is very common to the female sex,
and troublesome and vexatious, and it is
found in almost all now, of whatever station
they are, and is very closely related to gonorrhea.
It is sometimes without pain, also sometimes
with pain. It sends more often then until pain
of the lower back and in the loins, sometimes happening
cold feet, slight fevers, weakness in all limbs,
and when some matter is sharp and salty, it makes
a very bitter burning. The matter has a
difference from any initial flux, and the
most hideously stinking, which stick in the blood
and are afterwards expelled by nature.
If someone of the sex falls ill, after
40 or 50 years when the flux ceases, it
is almost hope too late that one
gets rid of it; but where after some time it
shows itself, there is still help to be had.
First it is to be noted that one should
cleanse the patient and purge with suitable remedies,
and then use the other assured remedies.
NB: that everyone should note that one should notNB: written in red ink
wish to heal or close this, if it only comes every
month after the flux for 2 or 3 days; if
however it continues, then one must do something about it
and not let it stand any longer.
If it is a simple white flux, then one can
use the remedies as in the fluxes of men
in gonorrhea.

On Disease of the WombRubricated heading in red ink framed by horizontal red double rules above and below; contains alchemical symbol ♀ (Venus/woman) with M:
The poor womenfolk are
afflicted by many troubles,
when some men are loose and free
therefrom; and the greatest concern of women
is what they have with the womb, and there is
none free or exempted: young folk,
rich and poor, of high and low station, know
to complain and speak of the womb.
And this organ, namely the womb, is subject to many
diseases and conditions, which
if I were to describe everything, would become a long

treatise; I will therefore only
mention a few things thereof.
The womb often troubles women from a
small and very slight cause, becoming turbulent
and rebellious, sometimes when they
only eat something sour or contrary to the womb,
or when they only smell something pleasant,
namely civet, musk, ambergris, roses,
jasmine, or similar costly fragrant things
comes into the nose, then some fall into complete
convulsions and fainting; but everything comes in a
similar manner. One will find many
womenfolk who in a very sudden
manner suffer or are afflicted, or in
a very similar manner are attacked.
And the fits are so many and various
that if I wanted to describe all, it would cause worry
that it would fill the volume; however I will
briefly state what is most notable.
The Plagues of Women concerning theRubricated heading in red ink
Womb are theseRubricated heading in red ink with flourish
Faintings with cold sweat, vomiting, yawning and
tearing in the belly, rumbling, obstruction of the
breath, pain of the head, convulsions, suffocation
under the breast, vapor in the right
hypochondrium, and heart palpitations, half-loss
of sight and cheeks, at times so strong that the
head and eyes darken as if she
should quite fall down and lie there without
a sign as if she were dead, cold hands
sometimes, and have movement from
one side not in their power; sometimes
they are quite cold, sometimes quite warm,
or a sweat comes upon them.

gather vapor and winds and some stinking poisons
which reside or consist in this sour evil
humor. So it is to be noted and understood
regarding this, that the vital spirits all

lower spirits, and they follow after the vital

hurrying others are brought at once to the heart and brain,
where with their stench they
disturb the spirits in both brain and heart
and bring confusion, since they
cannot endure these stinking vapors; thereupon

bad gathered moistures, and such are for the women
and the fruit very dangerous, so that it kills
the fruit in the mother's womb.
Therefore one should prescribe for such a woman a good diet,
so that it is directed to the fruit and the illness.
And if it is necessary that one must purge,
it should be done with manna and sweet syrups, as
already mentioned before by the doctor, and one can
hold it stronger or attack more; it should
be done from the fourth month until the seventh,
and not in the first three, nor the 3 last months.

The head is wounded in various ways, by blow,
hitting, hewing, thrusting, shots, etc.: however, the
places of the head are differently wounded;
one is more dangerous than the other.
The wounds on the anterior part of the head, also
those at the temples, when these are wounded,
even if they are so small, etc., they are yet more dangerous
than the wounds on the posterior part, or upon
the crown of the head. For at the tem-
ples lie principal muscles, and arte-
ries, which convey blood and vital
spirits to the brain, and none without injury to
life can be damaged. The anterior
cranium, because it is thin and friable, also
because of the cavity of the brain, where the spiri-
tus animales reside therein, therefore all
one should carefully observe which part is injured.

Wounds of the Chest –Rubricated heading in red ink
Wounds of the chest are various: some
are deep, and some go right into the cavity so that
sometimes even the internal organs
are injured. The external wounds are
without danger, since they are healed like other fresh
wounds; but those that go into the cavity
are all severe and dangerous, even if one
does not touch or injure the internal organs,
yet there is danger because of the accumulation of
clotted blood which has coagulated in the cavity, as
it putrefies and causes the greatest inconvenience.
Since chest wounds are located in cavities,
the wound on the chest is
mostly bad, however, when caused by a
rapier, knife, arrow, etc., so that it goes through
into the cavity. One will perceive it when
the breath passes through the wound, especially
when he holds mouth and nose shut; then
from the breath or when the wound is halfway inward
armeFaint catchword/mark at bottom right margin

frightens, or because of the air which is drawn inRed-ink top horizontal and central vertical divider rules frame the columns
through the wound or goes out;
as when too much blood has settled on his diaphragm
and weighs it down. Such wounds
are also quickly probed and found with a probe.
found.

with a good decoction.
