Of the Joint-Water (Synovia).Rubricated heading in red ink
The joint-water, called synovia, is the sap
of the human body, which through strong
[injury] of wounds is often brought to run
out, not differently from birch trees when
they let their sap run out. When thus this
sap runs out strongly in a person, then
the person dies thereof; or if it

turns out well, the injured limb withers
away. The joint-water is nothing else than the
evil sap of the white sinews; just as
blood is the sap of the red veins,
so the white sap [is] of the white sinews.
That however the joints have yet another sap
called gluten, which should not be the
joint-water, and yet not to be dis-
believed, is however brought forth from the flesh,
namely that which gluten is in
very little quantity in a person, and only so
much that the joints have their slippery
juiciness, and when such once
runs out, those same limbs stiffen, and
let themselves no longer be bent, and can also
by no art be brought back.
The joint-water is not to be bound up,
because as a thin water it is not fit
therefor; however it sometimes causes
a great [swelling/lump], which through great
pains are caused, and great holes
fall in.

Of various bone fractures,Rubricated heading in red ink
signs, and dangersRubricated heading in red ink
Bone fractures are very various, and one
more dangerous than the other, for there are 4
distinctions to note. First, when an arm or
leg is broken transversely in two, so that
one can bend and move the bone shafts to and fro,
with or without a wound, it is called fractura
or a true fracture. Secondly, when the bones
are shattered and many small splinters come off,
as if smashed with a hammer, then
this fracture is called a morpha or commi-
nutio. Since then the bone is broken into
the smallest pieces, so that splinters come
out, and the joint with the greatest skill
must be brought to its place and previous motion,
it may well be called ruined,
and is called a dismembered fracture.
The fourth kind is when the bone is split
along its length, as it were; this is fissura,
a cleft or slit fracture. The first, third,
and fourth kinds can happen without great injury
to the flesh, but the second cannot;
therefore the same is the most difficult of all to
cure. On account of great injury to the nerves
and the marrow, equally dangerous are fractures
in the joint, on account of great symptoms, contusion of the
nerves, etc., from which fatal symptoms arise
343Pencil foliation below body text

759Boxed page number in top right
can, such as great sensitivity, then
severe pain, heat, inflammation, bleeding,
and even gangrene. Yet if it goes
well and progresses, there commonly follows
stiffness, [especially] of the foot. Some
must afterwards limp, or indeed can no longer
bear weight, for to do as the
surgeon [who] in 8 days does not use a poultice/plaster,
but afterwards mixes my special Red
Plaster with half diaphoretic [plaster]
of Mynsicht, and thus prevents the above-mentioned
and the great defects in the bone
quietly heals. The other two [kinds], however,
transverse and longitudinal, can next to
God's help and diligent care well
be cured.
A fracture occurring in a large bone is worse
to cure than one in a small one; when both
shafts either of the shin or of the forearm
are in two, it is worse than when only
one alone is broken; a multiple
fracture with many splinters is more dangerous
to set right than a simple
one. Those with a wounding and
wound are far more dangerous than the others;
those near the shin, elbow, or ankle
are harder to heal than those in the middle of
the shafts, and finally a slit fracture is
more [curable/less severe] than a morpha.
The signs of a fracture areRubricated heading in red ink
First, when you can bend the bone to and fro.
2. When one leg/bone is shorter than
the other, and upon touching the fractured
bone one perceives a grating sound. Thirdly,
when there is no longer any strength in the limb,
so that one can no longer lift it up.
Fourthly, the patient feels at the
site of the fracture great pain when one
touches it, on account of the great sensitivity
of the injured nerves. Behind/Finally it is
worst of all when the patient [tells] the physician

The injury itself tells how it
happened, so that one can all the more easily
judge accordingly.
Fractures are much better to cure in winter
than in summer, because the humors
are too [strikethrough] dry than in summer,Strikethrough
for in hot times they do not willingly
heal together. Fractures in youth are
more easily and quickly healed than in
old age.

When you are called to such a patient,Initial 'W' written in red ink

After this, have one or 2 strong fellows

As I have seen in the world, one should
not unbind the patient before 4 or 5 days, and
see that the foot lies straight and still; there is nothing
worse than when one unbinds a leg fracture
often, and lays the patient crooked, and
changes the position; a moderate swelling
in a leg fracture is not very bad, for
there is no leg fracture that does not for 2 or 3 days
show a little swelling, during which appearance
beware always of greasing and moist things,
which the inflamed and swollen
limb cannot tolerate, but rather use
Giollat's Diapalma plaster; if however
the complications seem too furious and hot
to rise, open a vein, and use
often the golden milk; the bandages, as
mentioned before, must not be too long
or too narrow, for frayed and narrow
binding in fractures is harmful, therefore keep
the middle way, because Nature does not at all want
to be forced, but rather works
in its own way; therefore nothing other than inflammation
and gangrene, which one often
sees from unskillful bandaging, so that the swelling
appears beside the bandages,
followed by red blisters, also often indeed
brings something quite dreadful. When the

and you can bind it again at pleasure, examine

soon know of any mortification, or

How One Should Behave with Open FracturesRubricated heading in red ink
Where a Wound is Present,Rubricated heading in red ink
and in Comminuted Fractures.Rubricated heading in red ink
When a bone through great force is
broken, or the fall happened upon something sharp
or blunt, then it does not happen
without a wound, so that sometimes
the bare bone sticks out, the bone pieces
themselves without splinters, or indeed not detached,
broken into fragments; some can soon
be taken out, some however one must
leave to Nature until it detaches them,
or until one comes to aid with medicine and
detaches them; however it may happen,
begin your cure thus: First set the
bone upon one another as mentioned here before;
that must happen soon, before any
inflammation or swelling comes thereto;
for afterwards the setting can wholly and

no longer be accomplished, except with
greater pain, not without pain and
even spasm/convulsion follows thereon;
and if one sees the appearance of a great
swelling, and already an inflammation is present, then
a strong swelling and swollen
flesh, which happens after the fracture has occurred,
strikes; do not let yourself be frightened, therefore it is
best that one let it stand gently,
until through serviceable means the pain is stilled,
the swelling is dispersed, and the humors
are led out and consumed; after the
setting, unite the wound lips as much as
possible with an adhesive plaster,
so that the exposed bone is better covered
and receives no injury from the harmful air;
around the wound however lay a good
defensive plaster, yet so that always a
hole is made therein, as large as the wound
requires; and around the defensive plaster,
lay Felix Würtz's fracture plaster,
so that it can cover the remaining parts,
wherein also a hole should be cut,
so that the other plasters without the same
can be removed, and let this
lie still several days. The wound however bind
twice daily, like another wound,
with cleansing and healing remedies, and fasten the
lint/pledget, and lay always a thickly spread
bitumen/pitch plaster over it. After this prevent
above all things the inflammation; ward off
the hot humors, preserve the broken
bones unmoved together, and when
they by means of the callus are again
healed together, then close it properly with
drying medicaments, until complete
health. Should however a leg fracture have a
large piece sticking out so that even through
strong pulling and cords it were not possible
to bring it back in again, one can
with a convenient saw, or file, or other
convenient instrument, remove it, because it is
better that one removes it as an obstacle out of the
way, than that one by grasping too

Of Erysipelas or St. Anthony's FireRubricated heading in red ink
Erysipelas comes all too readily to wounds
and bone fractures, caused
which sometimes arises from neglect and
through unskillful medicine, unsuitable
remedies, when one does not
bandage it early enough, or it is indeed the patient's
own fault, that in eating and drinking he
does not conduct himself properly.
The signs of erysipelas are manifest: there
is no fixed hour; it comes with a
heat and chill, all the inflamed pain
in the limb with an inflamed and
bright-red shining, yellowish-tinted
color. In some, when it lasts long,
small blisters rise up or
millet-like pustules; and this is a sign
of erysipelas having gained the upper hand. Thereafter
holes often cave in. Where it is not
cured in time, to prevent
prolonged sores and chronic fluxes.
How often and frequently in old people even
gangrene (cold fire) arises, and extinguishes life
altogether. A certain diagnostic sign
is when one presses the spot with the finger
a little, the redness tends to
give way somewhat; when one
takes the finger away, however, the redness
immediately reappears.
The cure in erysipelas: the best remedy is
that one administers something to induce sweating; and
the best is a proper and good diaphoretic
antimony. Where, however, one does not
have this, then only elderberry rob with
elderflower water and blessed thistle water administered,
or else give the following:
Take: elderberry rob without vinegar, prepared aromatics 2 drams,
diaphoretic antimony 12 grains, bezoar 3 grains,
348Modern pencil foliation at bottom of column 1

779Boxed page number at top right
blessed thistle water 2 drams; mix with water
of elderflowers for a draught; give at one
time.
Or the following: Take: Andromachus's theriac
half a dram, mineral bezoar 15 grains, water
of elderflowers, with liquid chicory water;
mix for a draught and give at one time.
When this, along with an efficacious [evacuation]
of the body, has been used, then
external remedies may be applied. For
although I have recorded one and another
more in this book, yet not one and the same
thing and medicine for erysipelas is for all
constitutions; for one suits well, to others
ointments, to others cooling poultices
and compresses etc. Thus the physician must
be careful and take good heed that he
applies that which nature more
prefers and finds agreeable.
The following is a simple but proven
remedy: Take elderberry rob, mixed with
vinegar, spread on leather and laid over it; and it is
not sufficiently to be praised for its virtue.
If, however, the erysipelas has entered a true
course of treatment, one must use other remedies,

salves are to be strictly avoided here, because

heal up, and indeed from the very ground
regain health.
